title: The Generalised Causality Principle
abstract: The no-signalling principle lies at the heart of Bell-type experiments involving spacelike-separated parties. Although not all no-signalling correlations can be realized within quantum theory, the no-sinalling principle itself remains fundamental even for post-quantum theories, since its violation would imply superluminal signalling. In the spirit of device independent nature of the Bell inequalities, there has recently been growing interest in causal inequalities, which identify correlations admitting no causal explanation. Such correlations have been rigorously studied within the process-matrix formalism, which is built upon a constraint analogous to spacelike separation in Bell scenarios. We refer to this constraint as the single-interaction constraint, whereby each party interacts with the environment only once. Despite considerable effort, no fundamental guiding principle is currently known that characterizes the restrictions this constraint imposes on the correlations generated by Process Matrices. In this work, we address this gap by proposing a generalized causality principle for the bipartite case. We show that for certain cases, the generalised causality principle defines a strict subset of the set of all signalling correlations. This principle thus provides a fundamental limit on quantum and even post-quantum theories subject to the single-interaction constraint. By analogy with no-signalling, whose violation excludes certain causal structures among the parties, a violation of the generalised causality principle rules out a corresponding class of causal structures(causal structures with the single interaction constraint). More broadly, our techniques provide a general framework for deriving generalised causal constraints, applicable to a wide class of indefinite-causal-order scenarios.
summary: This paper introduces a Generalized Causality Principle (GCP) to constrain correlations in quantum and post-quantum theories based on a single-interaction constraint. Using process matrices, the authors show that this principle imposes non-trivial restrictions on achievable correlations, analogous to how no-signalling constrains quantum correlations. This provides a powerful, general framework for testing fundamental causal assumptions.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a fundamental, theory-independent restriction on correlations generated by processes constrained by a single interaction, analogous to the no-signalling principle in Bell tests.
main_result: The authors propose a 'generalised causality principle' (GCP) which defines a strict subset of all signalling correlations for certain cases, providing a fundamental limit on quantum and post-quantum theories.
method: The work utilizes General Probabilistic Theories (GPTs) formulated via process-matrix formalism, deriving constraints by analyzing the structure of bipartite process matrices under single-interaction constraints.
model_or_system: The model involves bipartite processes described by four-partite Hermitian matrices ($W_{AI A O B I B O}$), representing correlations between two parties (Alice and Bob) interacting with an environment.
key_observables: Correlation probabilities $p(ab|xy)$, the Generalised Causality Polytope, and the process matrix $W$.
important_parameters: The number of outcomes for the parties (e.g., $2 	imes 2$ vs $3 	imes 3$ outcomes).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the 'no restriction hypothesis' for GPTs and the definition of the single-interaction constraint.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the process matrix formalism and the single-interaction constraint, introduces the GCP, and then proves theorems showing that GCP imposes non-trivial restrictions on correlations, especially for larger outcome sets.
why_interesting: The framework of process matrices and causality constraints is highly relevant to understanding fundamental limits in quantum information, particularly when considering device-independent security or generalized causal structures beyond standard quantum mechanics.
